_about: Marketing-claim risk checks. Patterns are case-insensitive regular expressions matched against each claim or a block of copy. Not legal advice.

claims.advice: US: allowed if true and substantiated. EU: BPA is now banned in food-contact materials (Reg. 2024/3190), so presenting a legal requirement as a special feature risks being misleading. Prefer 'made without bisphenols, tested to …' with evidence, or drop it.

Vague and unprovable ('chemical-free' is false by definition). Regulators (FTC, ACCC, EU UCPD) treat these as misleading. Replace with specific, tested statements (e.g. 'free from intentionally added PFAS', 'tested to EN 14372').

EU: from 27 Sept 2026, generic environmental claims without recognised excellent environmental performance, and climate-neutral claims based on offsetting, are banned (Directive (EU) 2024/825). US: FTC Green Guides require qualification and substantiation. UK: CMA Green Claims Code. Use specific, quantified claims (e.g. '50% recycled PP, certified by …').

If the material is a bamboo/plant-fibre composite with melamine or other plastic binder, 'natural' or 'bamboo' wording is misleading, and in the EU the material itself is non-compliant. For PLA/bio-based plastics, state bio-based content with a certification (e.g. ASTM D6866 / EN 16785).

California prohibits 'biodegradable/degradable/decomposable' on plastic products. 'Compostable' needs certification (ASTM D6400 / EN 13432) and clear disposal qualifiers; durable tableware rarely qualifies. EU 2024/825 and FTC Green Guides apply.

US FTC: only unqualified if recycling facilities are available to a substantial majority of consumers; California SB 343 restricts the chasing-arrows symbol and recyclability claims. Multi-material products (silicone + PP) are rarely recyclable in practice. EU PPWR adds harmonised rules.

US: antimicrobial treated articles must use an EPA-registered treatment and may only claim to protect the product itself (no health claims) under FIFRA. EU: Biocidal Products Regulation 528/2012 treated-article labelling applies. 'Hygienic' needs substantiation.
This isn't a legal term. Back it with the actual compliance basis (e.g. 'complies with FDA 21 CFR 177.2600 and EU 1935/2004, LFGB tested').
You need supplier evidence (e.g. USP Class VI / ISO 10993 certification of the exact grade used). Without it, the claim is misleading.
Platinum-cured is a real curing system, but it says nothing on its own about safety. Keep supplier certification, and pair it with the actual compliance tests.
Substantiate with a dishwasher-resistance test (EN 12875) covering colour, print, warping and suction performance after the cycles.
Needs migration testing at microwave conditions. Never claim it for melamine, bamboo composites or metal.
Absolute claims need robust drop and abuse testing; prefer 'break-resistant (tested: 1.2 m drop × N)'.
These are among the most-disputed claims in reviews. Substantiate with defined tests (tip/shake/drop with liquid), or use 'spill-resistant'.
Needs documented, current endorsement from the named professionals (and disclosure of any payment, under FTC Endorsement Guides). Avoid implying medical benefit.
Developmental/health benefit claims (speech, oral-motor, preventing picky eating) need evidence. Keep them modest ('designed to support self-feeding') unless you have studies.

This must be true for every component (lids, suction bases, inks, packaging windows). Under many definitions silicone isn't a plastic, but some regulators and consumers disagree, so state the material explicitly.
These are generally fine as descriptive terms. Avoid implying official endorsement.
